Forecast calibration

How good is the Lahore weather forecast?

When a forecast says "40% chance of rain", does it rain on 40% of those days? Checked against real station measurements across 216 cities worldwide.

New here? How to read this report

When a forecast says “40% chance of rain”, it is making a checkable promise: across all the days it says 40%, it should rain on about 4 in 10 of them. This report collects years of forecasts, lines each one up against what a rain gauge actually measured, and reports whether the promise was kept.

Two numbers do most of the work. Calibration is honesty: when the forecast said 40%, how often did it rain? On the calibration charts, the dashed diagonal is a perfectly honest forecast. The skill score is usefulness: 0 means no better than always quoting the local average, 1 would be perfect, and anything above about 0.35 is genuinely worth acting on.

Pick your city with the globe or the search button above; every chart and verdict follows your selection. Sections marked with a fold hold the machinery — open them if you want to know how a number was made, not just what it is. Every term is defined in plain language in the glossary.

The gauge's calendar day could not be confirmed — 10

Station precipitation is a 24-hour total ending at an hour the observer chooses, which need not line up with the calendar day the forecast refers to. Each gauge is lined up against reanalysis rain at shifts of up to two days; where no shift wins in 90% of resamples of the record the convention is unknown, and guessing it would not add noise - it would produce a confidently wrong answer.

Arad (RO), Cordoba (ES), Douglas (IM), Izmir (TR), Mersin (TR), Nador (MA), Nottingham (GB), Palma (ES), Perth (AU), Saint Helier (JE)

The gauge barely tracks the regional weather — 1

Gauge and reanalysis rain rank the days too differently (rank correlation below 0.3) to date the record, which also casts doubt on the gauge itself.

Bandar Seri Begawan (BN)

The record contradicts its own timestamps — 2

These gauges report the time of each observation, which fixes the calendar day. Their rain nevertheless lines up confidently with a different day, so either the timestamps or the record are wrong. They are left out rather than shifted.

Auckland (NZ), Christchurch (NZ)

The gauge misses most of the rain — 1

Over the same days the gauge records less than a third of the rain the ERA5 reanalysis puts at its location, so it is not measuring the city's rain.

Barranquilla (CO)

No usable record at all — 2

The station, the reanalysis or the forecast archive returned nothing overlapping the evaluation window.

Chisinau (MD), Gibraltar (GI)

The short answer for Lahore

The Lahore rain forecast is moderately skilful, though 4 points on its probability scale are off by more than chance explains.

When it says rain is near certain (98%), believe about 69%. When it says rain is very unlikely (0%), there is still roughly a 2% chance.

Based on 747 days, 2024-04-26 to 2026-05-31. "Rain" means at least 0.2 mm measured at the station, 1.9 km from the forecast grid point. Skill score 0.21, ranked 153 of 216 — but see the rank range (90–184) before reading anything into that position.

Is Bucharest unusual? The other European capitals #

One city cannot tell you whether a forecast is good or merely typical. The identical pipeline was therefore run over every European capital with a usable rain gauge. Of 43 capitals probed, 19 had a station close enough and current enough, and 18 survived the data checks once the records arrived.

Bucharest ranks 7 of 18 (skill 0.41), but the honest statement is the rank range: 4–10. With about two years per city, most of the ordering is not resolvable, and a league table with a winner would be reading noise. The rank column is deliberately a range for every city.

The calibration curves and the skill-against-rain-frequency scatter for every verified city — capitals included — are drawn once, interactively, in the world-cities section below, where they follow whichever city you have selected instead of keeping Bucharest in red for everyone.

The same bias appears in every capital. Low-probability days rain more often than stated in 16 of 18 capitals with a confidence interval excluding zero, and high-probability days rain less often than stated in 16 of 18. So the reversal of the published consumer "wet bias" is not a Bucharest quirk — it is what this forecast chain does everywhere, and it is the strongest evidence here that we are looking at raw model output rather than a hand-tuned product. Bucharest happens to be one of the mildest cases at the low end (+0.2%); the most extreme is Sarajevo at +59.1%.

What explains the spread?

Almost entirely how often it rains. Skill falls as the base rate rises (correlation -0.67, permutation p = 0.004): the wet Atlantic capitals are genuinely harder, not badly served. Distance from the gauge to the forecast grid point explains nothing at all (+0.23, p = 0.31), which is reassuring — it means the ranking is not an artefact of which cities happen to have a close station.

This cuts against the intuition behind ForecastWatch's "maritime locations are more predictable" framing. On a categorical accuracy rate, a dry climate scores well by saying "dry"; on a skill score, which removes that advantage, the maritime capitals come out worse, and Reykjavik — where it rains 77% of days — cannot beat its own climatology at all.

And temperature, for scale

The same capitals, on daily-max temperature error against lead time. The median capital sits at 1.05 °C one day ahead and 2.17 °C seven days ahead, once each site's constant offset is removed. meteoblue publish 1.66 °C for the best raw model at day one globally, so this archive is in the expected place — a reassurance that nothing in the pipeline is quietly broken. Error grows with lead time at much the same rate everywhere; the level differs, the slope barely does. The curves themselves are drawn once, interactively, in the world-cities section, with your selected city picked out.

Whose forecast is this, actually?

A league table only means something if every row is the same forecaster. It was not. Open-Meteo's default best_match picks a model per location, and across these capitals it resolves to ICON-EU in 9 of them and ECMWF IFS in 9. That identification is not inferred from a correlation: across three widely separated months the default series matches the pinned model's value in every single hour. Probability of precipitation is strongly model-dependent — at Bucharest, over identical days, ICON scores 0.41 and ECMWF 0.30 — so this had every opportunity to be the real reason one city outranked another.

The entire table was therefore rebuilt twice, pinning one model everywhere:

The ranking survives. Bucharest sits at 8 of 18 with ICON pinned everywhere and 7 of 18 with ECMWF pinned, against 7 as published. The gap between the ICON-served and ECMWF-served groups is +0.01 skill as published and -0.03 with the model held fixed — essentially unchanged. Model and geography were confounded, but the geography is what does the work: best_match sends ECMWF to the wet Atlantic capitals, and those really are harder.

The exercise paid for itself in a different way. ICON's advantage is not uniform — it tracks how often it rains (r = −0.64, p = 0.010). The high-resolution regional model wins where rain is infrequent and largely convective (Vienna +0.16, Bucharest +0.10), and loses where fronts arrive off the ocean (Dublin +0.03). Neither model is simply better, which is presumably why the default routes by region at all.

This came out of an audit, not luck. The study pins its model explicitly for temperature, but the probability series was requested without a model parameter and so silently inherited the default. Checking month by month showed the backing model never changed mid-archive, so no published number was built from a spliced series — but nothing except this check was guaranteeing that.

What was thrown away, and why

The exclusions are part of the result. Two capitals were rejected before any data was downloaded because their nearest qualifying gauge sits on a mountain (Andorra la Vella's is at 2451 m, Vaduz's at 2502 m); verifying a valley city against those would measure the lapse rate, not the forecast. The rest failed once their records were inspected:

  • Chisinau — no overlapping days

The rain-day convention had to be re-derived for every city separately, and it genuinely differs: the station date needs shifting back a day in Bucharest, Reykjavik and Sarajevo, and not at all elsewhere. Each shift is found by rank correlation against reanalysis rain and kept only if it wins in at least 90% of block-bootstrap resamples; assuming Bucharest's convention travelled would have produced confident, wrong curves.

Beyond the capitals: 216 cities #

Capitals are a biased sample — they are where the good instruments are. Widening to every city with a usable rain gauge tests whether the previous section's conclusions were about weather forecasting or about capitals.

The selection rule is unchanged and mechanical: a gauge within 25 km, within 300 m of the forecast grid point's elevation, reporting through the verification period. 230 cities passed that screen; 216 then survived the per-city rain-day convention scan and the record-quality checks. Cities sharing a gauge are counted once, so these remain independent samples.

Bucharest ranks 51 of 216 with skill 0.41 — rank range 21–92. Its score is unchanged to three decimals from the single-city and capitals runs, which is the regression test for this whole expansion: adding 215 cities did not perturb the original answer.

In the median city, days promised around 1% rain actually rain 5% of the time — while days promised 96% rain deliver only 77%.

Which of the 15-city findings survived

ExplainingDriver 15 capitals216 citiesReplication
bsshow often it rains-0.67 (p=0.004)-0.20 (p=0.004)held
bsscontinentality+0.09 (p=0.688)+0.42 (p=0.000)did not hold

reliabilitygauge distance-0.20 (p=0.323)+0.09 (p=0.223)held

The honest headline of this section is a failure to replicate. Across 15 capitals, skill looked as though it were largely dictated by how often it rains (r = −0.77, p = 0.001) — a tidy story. At 216 cities that correlation collapses to roughly −0.11 and is no longer distinguishable from chance. It was a small-sample artefact, and had this study stopped at the capitals it would have been reported as a result.

What does survive is the less convenient relationship: calibration error grows with the rain rate (r = +0.56, p < 0.001). Wetter cities are not forecast with less skill, but their stated probabilities sit further from the truth. Gauge distance still explains nothing, which continues to rule out the obvious measurement artefact.

How often it rains says almost nothing about how well rain is forecast (r = -0.20 across 216 cities).

The inversion is not a European quirk either

Low-probability days produce rain more often than stated in 166 of 216 cities (135 with a confidence interval excluding zero), and high-probability days produce rain less often in 203 of 216 (185 significant) — the opposite of the wet bias documented for consumer forecasts in the literature.

The sharper test is the 129 cities outside Europe — Sydney, Montreal, New York, Mexicali and others. They lie outside ICON-EU's domain, so a different model entirely is answering the request. The low-end under-forecasting still appears in 79 of 129 of them (55 significant). Across 15 European capitals this could have been a property of two European models; it now looks like a property of how this kind of forecast is made.

72% of cities understate low rain chances and overstate high ones — the same squeeze, almost everywhere.

Temperature error vs lead time

The deterministic track over the same cities, as daily-max error after removing each site's constant bias: a median of 1.10 °C at one day ahead, rising to 2.15 °C at seven.

A 7-day-ahead forecast of the daily high is about 2.0× as wrong as tomorrow's: 1.1 °C grows to 2.1 °C in the median city.

This covers 217 of the 216 cities, not all of them: the deterministic track is the most request-hungry step in the study and runs into the weather API's hourly quota. It stops cleanly and keeps what it has rather than discarding the run, so the figure is a partial but unbiased slice — cities are processed alphabetically, which is unrelated to forecast quality.

How to read this table. Skill (the Brier Skill Score) answers one question in everyday terms: how much better is this forecast than just quoting the local average? Higher is better; 0 means no better than that average, 1 is perfect. The rank range is the honest part: with about two years of data, most neighbouring ranks cannot be told apart, so a model "ranked 2–4" is not ranked second. Avg error is the average gap between promised and delivered rain chances, in percentage points.

Two of these “different providers” are one forecast. Every pair of models was compared hour by hour at every city, on the raw numbers as served, before any averaging could smooth a difference away: MET Norway returns the same rain probability as ECMWF IFS 0.25° — not similar, identical, to the last digit, at 18 cities. So the duplicate was merged into the other before ranking. Leaving it in would have given one forecast two places in the table, and made its agreement with itself look like two providers independently agreeing. Where a merge happened, the surviving row names the other label underneath. Nobody discloses this; it only showed up because the numbers were checked against each other.
Held-fixed check. individual values shift under pinning but the city ordering survives, so the published ranking measures geography, not routing.
Which model is my weather app actually using? Often, nobody will tell you — and it can change without notice. This study's provenance audit found that the "default" forecast service it buys from silently routes each city to a different underlying model: across the capitals probed, it resolved to ICON-EU in 10 of them and ECMWF IFS in 9, with no disclosure either way. At Bucharest, over identical days, that choice alone is worth +0.10 in skill. The audit only caught it because the default series was compared, hour by hour, against forecasts pinned to a named model. Your app almost certainly does the same thing, one layer further removed.
The Bucharest deep dive Hourly honesty, frost and heat odds, benchmarks and limits — analyses that need records only Bucharest has.

The Bucharest deep dive #

Everything below this line is Bucharest, whichever city you selected above. These analyses need hourly present-weather reports, a second station for the representativeness floor, and a temperature record long enough to derive frost and heat probabilities. Those exist for Bucharest and not for the other capitals, so the sections are not relabelled to match your selection — that would be inventing results. You currently have Lahore selected; its own results are above.

Is that actually good? #

Each bar shows where this forecast lands. Shaded regions are rules of thumb, not official thresholds — the raw number is always shown alongside.

Seasonal calibration curves

I expected summer to be worst, because summer rain here is convective — small, short-lived cells a forecast grid cannot resolve. It is not; spring is. Summer does have the weakest resolution, which is the convective signal, but its low rain rate makes the overall score look better.

Will it rain at 6pm? The hourly check #

Everything above asks "will it rain today". That is the easier and less useful question. This section asks whether the forecast is honest hour by hour — and because there are 10,696 hours instead of 731 days, the answer is far better supported.

 Daily Hourly
Sample731 days 10696 hours
Effective sample 3631665
Skill score (higher better) 0.409 0.467
Average error (lower better) 6.5%2.5%
What "almost certain" really means 82% 97%
The confident end is honest after all. On the daily view, "99%" meant 82% — apparent overconfidence. Hour by hour, "98%" means 97%, which is within the range a flawless forecast would give.

Read that carefully — it is not a clean comparison. Three things change at once between the two tracks: the event (at least 0.2 mm accumulated, versus precipitation simply being observed), the station, and the kind of measurement (a rain gauge versus an observer's present-weather report). A brief shower registers as precipitation hour-by-hour while depositing less than 0.2 mm in the gauge. So the most defensible reading is that much of the daily "overconfidence" was an artefact of the rain threshold, not dishonesty in the forecast — consistent with the threshold sensitivity seen in the robustness table.

The low end still misses: hours forecast at 0.5% see precipitation 2.4% of the time, and hours forecast at 13% see it 27% of the time. Both are genuinely outside chance. Low probabilities are understated at every timescale tested.

A caveat found while building this

The three Bucharest stations disagree sharply about how often it rains — and the pattern follows how often each one files a report, not how far it is from the city centre:

StationDistance Reports per hourHours with precipitation
Bucuresti Filaret1.1 km1.05.7%
Baneasa Aurel Vlaicu8.5 km1.310.2%
Henri Coanda / Otopeni16.1 km1.310.5%

The closest station reports the least rain, because it files the fewest reports and so misses brief showers between them. This is observing practice, not weather, and it sets a floor on how precisely any of this can be measured.

Could we just correct it?

If the extremes are overconfident, an obvious fix is to learn a correction. The honest way to measure its value is to train it on some days and test it on different days — otherwise the correction simply memorises the noise and always appears to help.

VersionBrier score Skill score
As published0.1171 0.409
Corrected, tested on unseen days 0.1169 0.410
Result: correcting it gains 0.16%. Essentially nothing. The overconfidence at the extremes is real, but it is small enough — and our record short enough — that a correction learned from 731 days is itself too noisy to help. Both facts matter: the bias exists, and chasing it is not worth it yet.

Does the conclusion survive poking at it?

A result is only worth reporting if it does not depend on arbitrary choices. These runs change the definition of "it rained", and swap the source of truth entirely, then check whether the overconfidence is still there.

What was changed "0%" really means"99%" really means Skill scoreConclusion
threshold 0.1 mm (variant)6%84%0.429held
threshold 0.2 mm (primary)5%82%0.409held
threshold 1.0 mm (variant)2%72%0.258held
truth = ERA5 reanalysis3%99%0.515flipped
truth = Baneasa station (10km)4%84%0.433held
Held in 4 of 5 variants. The overconfidence at both ends is not an artefact of how rain was defined or which station was used.

Note the ERA5 row: scored against a model-based reconstruction instead of a real gauge, the forecast looks considerably better (skill 0.52). That is the flattery effect of grading a model against another model — and the reason real measurements are used as the primary truth here.

How does this compare with what is already published?

There is no public calibration number for Bucharest — that is the gap this study fills — but there are published accuracy numbers for Europe. ForecastWatch scores 593 European locations on the share of high and low temperature forecasts landing within 3 °F (1.67 °C), and reports a country-level band of roughly 58%–70%. Computing the same quantity here puts the result on a scale someone else has already calibrated.

ForecastLead Temps within 1.67 °C …after removing site bias Day-max error (°C) Rain/no-rain correct
ecmwf_ifs025145%64%1.5982%
icon_eu148%66%1.2683%
persistence144%44%2.6974%
ecmwf_ifs025244%60%1.7280%
icon_eu245%61%1.4679%
persistence233%33%3.8065%
ecmwf_ifs025343%54%1.8177%
icon_eu342%57%1.6179%
persistence328%28%4.2464%

Raw, the day-1 rate is 45% — below the published band. Almost all of that is one fixed offset: the grid point runs +2.5 °C too warm overnight against the Baneasa gauge, while daytime highs are only -0.9 °C off. Subtract that constant and the rate becomes 64%, inside the band. Every provider in the ForecastWatch panel post-processes its output, and removing a site offset is the first thing such post-processing does, so the debiased column is the fairer comparison — though it is fitted on the same days it is scored on, so read it as a ceiling.

Against "tomorrow will be like today". At lead 1 the model beats persistence only narrowly on this tolerance metric (45% vs 44%), because persistence has no site bias to speak of. Its advantage is unmissable elsewhere: day-max error 1.59 °C vs 2.69 °C, rain calls 82% vs 74%, and the gap widens with every extra day of lead.

A hit rate is a weak measure of a probability forecast, which is why it is not the headline here. The rain probabilities score 85% correct when thresholded at 50% — but simply saying "dry" every single day scores 73%, because it only rains on 27% of days. The Brier score above does not have that blind spot.

Does Bucharest show the classic "wet bias"?

The best-known result in this area (Bickel & Kim, 2008) is that a consumer weather provider over-states low rain chances: on days it calls 10%, it rains less often than that. Stating the expectation first turns the curve into a test rather than a story told after the fact.

Days where…Days StatedActually rained Gap (95% CI)
low (PoP <= 20%)475 3.1% 7.4% +4.3% [+2.1%, +7.0%]
high (PoP >= 60%)167 88.0% 76.0% -11.9% [-18.8%, -5.9%]
The opposite happens here. Low-probability days rain more often than stated (+4.3%), and high-probability days rain less often (-11.9%); both intervals exclude zero, and they come from a block bootstrap that respects week-long dry spells rather than pretending consecutive days are independent. That is the signature of raw model output, not of a consumer product: nobody has nudged the low end upward to avoid being blamed for a surprise shower.

Caveat that must travel with these numbers: ForecastWatch uses its own provider panel, station set and quality control, and publishes at country level. A figure landing inside their band is consistent with their measurement, not equal to it. This is positioning, not a ranking.

Frost, heat and rain — and how far ahead each is worth trusting #

Everything so far has been about rain, because rain is the only thing the archive attaches a probability to. But you might reasonably want a probability of frost tonight, or of a 35 C scorcher next week. Those can be worked out from the plain temperature forecast, and then checked the same way.

Read this section differently from the others. The probabilities here were not published by anyone — they were derived from the ordinary temperature and rainfall forecast by learning, from past days, how often each forecast value was followed by the event. So the fact that they come out well calibrated is not a finding: they were built to be. What cannot be faked is resolution and skill — how sharply the forecast separates days when the event happens from days when it does not. That is what the table below shows. Each day was scored by a recipe trained only on other, non-adjacent stretches of time, never on itself.

Skill score by event and days ahead

EventHow often Days ahead
1234567
Hot day (max temp >= 32 C)13%0.840.860.850.820.790.710.66
Extreme heat (max temp >= 35 C)6%0.700.650.680.640.570.470.48
Frost (min temp < 0 C)25%0.700.710.670.640.660.630.56
Rain (>= 0.2 mm)27%0.460.360.330.260.220.150.12

1.00 = perfect, 0.00 = no better than quoting the long-run average for the time of year. Each column is 812 days.

Temperature events stay predictable far longer than rain. Hot day (max temp >= 32 C) is at 0.84 a day ahead and still 0.66 a week out. Rain (>= 0.2 mm) starts lower (0.46) and collapses to 0.12 — close to useless. A week-ahead warning about temperature is worth acting on; a week-ahead rain forecast is barely worth reading.

Because the probability is derived, the recipe could be doing the work rather than the forecast. Two quite different recipes were tried — one assuming a fixed S-shaped curve, one assuming only "more never means less". They disagree by at most 0.063 in skill, so the ranking above is a property of the forecast, not of the method.

Extreme heat is the thinnest result here: only 48 such days occurred in the whole record, so treat its numbers as indicative.

What this does not tell you #

  • One lead time only, for the published rain probability. The rain results above cover a short-range forecast, so they do not tell you how far ahead a published probability can be trusted. The frost-and-heat section answers that question for derived probabilities, but those are not what a weather app shows you. A daily logger is accumulating the data for the real thing.
  • We have less evidence than it looks. 731 days sounds like a lot, but weather persists, so the effective sample is about 363 independent days.
  • The gauge is a point, the forecast is a square. The two stations, 10 km apart, disagree about whether it rained on 7.4% of days. No calibration claim finer than that is meaningful. See representativeness.
  • Temperature degrades with lead time, from 1.58 °C average error at 1 day to 2.64 °C at 7 days, with a persistent cold bias at short range.
Who actually makes these forecasts? The models behind the app — and why the label on the app is not the name of the forecaster.

Who makes these forecasts? #

Every weather app gets its numbers from a weather model run by a national weather service or an international centre. There is no single "the forecast": at last count this study tracks 15 models from 11 organisations, and they routinely disagree.

The concepts, in one minute

A weather model is a computer simulation of the atmosphere: it cuts the world into grid squares, applies the laws of physics step by step, and turns today's observations into a forecast. Two different computers, given the same starting observations, produce different rain probabilities for the same city — because they use different grid sizes, different shortcuts for physics too small to simulate, and different judgements about how to blend observations in. Neither is lying; they are different approximations of the same impossibly hard problem. Verification is how we tell which approximations are actually better: compare what was promised against what a rain gauge measured, over many days.

The organisations behind the models

Why do their forecasts differ? Partly geography: a model built to resolve European thunderstorms says little about the Pacific. Partly philosophy: the American and European centres make different trade-offs between resolution, range and computing cost. And partly chance: small differences at the start of a simulation grow into different pictures of whether a front arrives tonight or tomorrow morning.

ECMWF

An intergovernmental centre owned by more than thirty European countries, based in Reading, England. It does not serve the public directly - most weather apps buy its output - but its global model is widely treated as the reference that others measure themselves against.

  • ECMWF IFS 0.25° — The European intergovernmental weather centre's global model - widely regarded as the reference global forecast. archive verified in 19 cities probed
DWD (German Weather Service)

Germany's national weather service. Its models cover Europe at much finer detail than the global models manage, which is why it tends to win in the middle of Europe and matter less further away.

  • ICON-EU — Germany's weather service's high-resolution model covering Europe; sharper detail than global models inside its area. archive verified in 19 cities probed
  • ICON-D2 — Germany's very-high-resolution model for Germany and the immediate surroundings; short range only. archive verified in 6 cities probed
NOAA (US National Weather Service)

The United States' weather agency. Its global model, the GFS, is the other big worldwide forecaster alongside the European one - the two disagree regularly, and forecasters watch both.

  • GFS — The United States' global model; the other big global forecaster alongside ECMWF. archive verified in 19 cities probed
Météo-France

France's national weather service, running both a global model and a sharply detailed European one focused on France and its neighbours.

  • ARPEGE World — France's weather service global model.
  • AROME France — France's high-resolution model covering France and nearby countries.
  • AROME France HD — The higher-resolution variant of Météo-France's French model.
Met Office (UK)

The United Kingdom's weather service, one of the oldest in the world, with its own global model and a very fine-grained model over the British Isles.

  • UKMO Global — The United Kingdom's weather service global model. archive verified in 19 cities probed
  • UKMO UK 2 km — The Met Office's very-high-resolution model over the British Isles. archive verified in 5 cities probed
ECCC (Environment Canada)

Canada's national weather service. Its global model is built for a continent of extremes, from Arctic cold to hurricane season.

  • GEM — Canada's weather service global model. archive verified in 19 cities probed
Japan Meteorological Agency

Japan's national weather service, renowned for typhoon forecasting and one of the few agencies running a truly global model independently of the US and Europe.

  • JMA — Japan's weather service global model.
MET Norway

Norway's national weather service, whose open model chain is widely used across the Nordic countries.

  • MET Norway — Norway's weather service model chain. archive verified in 19 cities probed
KNMI (Netherlands)

The Dutch weather service. Its high-resolution European model is shared with several neighbouring countries, so the same forecast engine appears under several national flags.

  • HARMONIE (KNMI) — The Dutch weather service's high-resolution European model, shared with several neighbouring services.
DMI (Denmark)

The Danish weather service, running the same shared high-resolution European model as the Netherlands for the Danish region.

  • HARMONIE (DMI) — The Danish weather service's run of the same high-resolution European model.
ARPAE (Italy)

Italy's environmental protection agency, whose high-resolution model covers Italy and southern Europe.

  • COSMO 5 km — Italy's environmental agency's high-resolution model over southern Europe.

Model descriptions come from the study's provider registry (src/config.py); archive availability per city is measured, not assumed, by src/probe_providers.py.

The number you see vs the raw ensemble What Open-Meteo's probability is made from, and whether the processing helped.

The number you see, against the raw ensemble #

Every probability on this page so far has been taken at face value and scored. This section asks a different question: where does it come from? No provider documents how its rain probability is computed. So we rebuilt one the way a forecaster would — take the American ensemble's 31 members, count how many produce rain, publish the fraction — and put the two side by side on 108,163 city-days across 195 cities.

Days ahead Served saysEnsemble says GapTypical distance Agreement
140%50%-0.0930.1440.84
240%49%-0.0900.1590.82
340%49%-0.0870.1770.79
440%49%-0.0870.2000.75
540%49%-0.0870.2240.70
640%49%-0.0890.2450.66
740%50%-0.0930.2640.62

The served number is consistently the drier of the two, and the two drift apart as the forecast reaches further out: at a week ahead they are barely related to each other. That is a description of the pipeline, not yet a verdict on it — drier could mean better.

Is the served number better calibrated? It depends what you mean by a rainy day.

At one day ahead, the only lead where the comparison is clean, the served number is the more accurate of the two by 0.0197 (interval -0.0225 to -0.0170, p = 0.001), allowing for the fact that weather persists for days and that 195 cities share the same weather systems. That looks like a clean win.

It survives exactly one change of definition. Scored instead against the event the served number actually answers — rain at any point in the day, rather than a day-total crossing the threshold — the sign reverses: the raw ensemble is ahead by 0.0036 (p = 0.001). Both directions are firmly resolved, so this is not the data being too thin to tell. Which forecast is ‘better calibrated’ depends on which of two defensible definitions of a rainy day you pick — and neither the app nor the score tells you which one was used.

Where it does matter: the person who acts on cheap precautions

Average accuracy is an average over users. Consider instead someone whose protective action is nearly free relative to the damage it prevents — bring the washing in, carry an umbrella — who should therefore act on quite low probabilities. Measured as the fraction of the achievable benefit each forecast actually delivers to that user:

Cost of acting, vs. cost of being caught out Served numberRaw ensemble Difference
1 in 20 (act on ~5% chance) -0.28 +0.04 -0.32 (p = 0.001)
1 in 10 (act on ~10% chance) +0.14 +0.25 -0.12 (p = 0.001)
1 in 2 (act on ~50% chance) +0.41 +0.35 +0.07 (p = 0.001)

A negative number means following the forecast leaves the user worse off than a standing habit of always acting, or never acting. At the cheapest action the served probability is not merely less useful than the ensemble — it is worse than useless, while the ensemble roughly breaks even; and the dry bias in the table above is why, because a number that runs low never crosses a low threshold. The gap narrows as acting gets more expensive, and by the halfway point it has closed.

The two findings belong together, and they point opposite ways. On average accuracy the served number wins; on the same days, for the cheap-action user, it loses heavily. Both are resolved, so a reader told ‘better calibrated’ and a reader who acts on small chances would be given contradictory advice from one sample. Which is the point: the choice of measure, not the amount of data, decides whether a reader ever sees the harm.

Whether it rains, versus how much

One last split, and the only one on this page that leaves the rain probability behind. Each forecast series is scored twice — once on whether rain occurred, once on how much fell — against the same reference: a same-day-of-year climatology, what the calendar alone would have told you.

Sample Will it rain? How much will fall?
SkillBeat it SkillBeat it
15 capitals, several providers each (72 series)+0.29790%-0.06336%
104 cities worldwide, one provider each (191 series)+0.27885%-0.06938%

Forecasting is decisively better than the calendar at the yes/no question and worse than the calendar at the amount, in both samples. Rainfall totals are the harder problem, and the credibility a well-behaved rain probability earns does not transfer to the millimetres printed next to it.

Where the numbers come from Provenance: the archive, the stations, the licences, and what was verified rather than assumed.

What is the number, before anyone scores it? #

Everything above treats the published probability as a given and asks whether it is any good. This section asks something prior and less comfortable: is it the thing you think it is? Four checks, none of which needs a single observation of the weather.

1. Two names, one forecast

Every pair of models was compared hour by hour on the raw values as served, before any daily reduction could launder a difference away — 354 comparisons on the probability alone.

PairChannel CitiesHours Identical
ecmwf_ifs025 = metno_seamlessprobability19 / 1920,760100%
ukmo_seamless = ukmo_uk_deterministic_2kmamount5 / 520,880100%
ukmo_seamless = ukmo_uk_deterministic_2kmprobability5 / 52,272100%
MET Norway serves ECMWF's probability. Not similar to it — the same number, to the last digit, on 20,760 hours at every one of 19 cities. Its rainfall amounts are its own: identical on 80% of hours, differing by up to 22.2 mm. So a test demanding that two models match on both channels would have called this pair distinct and missed the duplication in the one field this study scores. Duplication is a property of the field you are reading, not of the model's name.

The cut is checked rather than trusted: every flagged pair sits at exactly 100%, nothing at all lands between 99% and 99.9%, and the closest unflagged pair is 98.37%. Any threshold in that empty band gives this same answer. A reader counting providers is counting fewer independent opinions than the menu suggests.

2. The number is rounded before you see it

The served probability takes 101 distinct values — whole percentage points. That rounding is not free, but it is also not the explanation for anything here: re-deriving the vendor's own daily figure at three-hourly resolution moves it by a median of 0.00, with a 99th percentile of 0.36. Small in the middle, occasionally large in the tail, so it is reported as a distribution rather than waved away with an average.

3. Is the archive the same as the source?

The raw-ensemble comparison leans on a third party's republication of NOAA's data, which is an obvious thing to distrust. So it was checked against NOAA's own GRIB2 files, byte-range by byte-range: 180 comparisons, mean absolute difference 0.0012 mm, largest 0.04 mm, 105 of them bit-exact, and 0 days where the two disagree about whether it rained.

Two raw values come back slightly negative (-0.04 mm), an artefact of the rounded-mantissa compression rather than of the weather. Disclosed rather than clipped silently, because a reader who finds it themselves is entitled to wonder what else was tidied.

4. Who owns it

12 input sources, each read from its own licence page rather than from a summary of one. 1 of them is share-alike, and tracing which published files inherit that term turned up a file republishing its output as served values rather than as a statistic — the larger obligation, and one that a scan of the forecast registry alone would have missed. The full record, with the wording, the URL and the date each was read, is in NOTICE.md.

Auditing our own compliance found the first failure: this site named its data source in plain text on every page without the link the licence requires. That is fixed, and the build now fails on any page that regresses.

Work with us #

Consulting · pipelines, telemetry, verification

Shipping a number is easy.
Proving it was true is the job.

DevOps hands, an engineering degree and a scientist's refusal to take a metric on trust. I build the boring half — collection, automation, infrastructure that survives being left alone — then do the half almost everyone skips: score what the system promised against what actually happened, with intervals. Here the promise is a rain probability; elsewhere it is an SLO, a vendor's accuracy claim or a model in production. The rig below does not care which — and it is the rig that produced every number on this page.

  1. Collect 5 × 18 models × cities, one API quota Rate-limited APIs, resumable cache, months of unattended runs. Re-running it is boring, which is the whole point.
  2. Reconcile 10,696 hourly forecasts to gauges Forecast meets ground truth. A join that quietly drops rows is a lie with a timestamp on it, so this one fails loudly instead.
  3. Score 88% → 76% promised vs. delivered Skill, calibration and bootstrap intervals. Uncertainty stated in the open, so the finding survives someone arguing with it.
  4. Publish 1 command rebuilds this page byte for byte An answer nobody can reproduce next quarter was never an answer. This page is the regression test for its own conclusions.

Caught by this rig: a weather API silently routing 19 capitals to different underlying models, undisclosed. That is the class of thing verification finds and a status page never will.

How this analysis could be improved Known weaknesses, in the order they matter.
Glossary Every term on this page, in plain language.

Glossary #

Every technical term used above, in plain language.

PoP — Probability of Precipitation

The number behind "30% chance of rain". It means: across many days that look like this one, it rains on about 30% of them.

It does NOT mean rain over 30% of the city, or for 30% of the day. That misreading is extremely common.
Calibration — also: reliability

Whether those percentages are honest. Take every day the forecast said 30%, and check how often it actually rained. If it is close to 30%, the forecast is calibrated.

A calibration curve just does this for every percentage at once. Points on the diagonal = honest. Below = overpromising rain.
Base rate — climatology

How often it simply rains here, ignoring any forecast.

This is the no-skill baseline. You could say this number every single day and be perfectly calibrated while being useless - which is why calibration alone is not enough.
Brier score — BS

Average squared miss between the promised probability and what happened (1 = it rained, 0 = it did not). Lower is better.

Brier scores are NOT comparable between places. A desert forecaster who always says 2% scores a brilliant Brier score while telling you nothing. That is why the skill score exists.
Brier Skill Score — BSS

How much better than just quoting the long-run average. Higher is better; 1.0 is perfect.

This is the number that actually answers "is the forecast any good?". Operational day-ahead rain forecasts typically land between 0.3 and 0.5.
Reliability term — the honesty penalty

The part of the Brier score caused purely by percentages being dishonest. Zero is perfect.

Compare it to the uncertainty term to judge size. Here it is a few percent of it, which is small.
Resolution term — the discrimination reward

How much the forecast actually separates rainy days from dry ones. Higher is better, capped by the uncertainty term.

This is what proves the forecast is not just hedging toward the base rate every day. Calibration without resolution is useless.
Uncertainty term — difficulty of the problem

How hard forecasting rain is here at all, fixed by the local climate. Not a measure of forecast quality.

It peaks at 0.25 for a 50/50 event. A place where it always or never rains is trivially easy and scores near zero.
ECE — Expected Calibration Error

The average gap between what was promised and what happened, in percentage points. The most directly readable calibration number.

Under 5 points is excellent, 5-10 is good, above 15 is poor.
Sharpness

Willingness to commit to confident numbers like 5% or 95%, instead of mumbling "40%" every day.

Not accuracy - it is the companion to calibration. A useful forecast needs both: honest AND decisive.
Consistency range — perfect-forecast range

How far off the diagonal a point would land even if the forecast were flawless, purely because we only have a limited number of days.

This is what separates real miscalibration from noise. A point inside this range is NOT evidence of a problem, however far from the diagonal it looks.
Effective sample size

How many genuinely independent days we have, which is fewer than the calendar days we collected.

Weather persists: if it rained today it probably rained yesterday. Consecutive days are not independent evidence, so all error bars must use this smaller number.
Block bootstrap

The method used for the error bars. It resamples the data in multi-day chunks rather than single days.

Resampling single days would assume they are independent and produce error bars that are far too narrow.
Isotonic recalibration

Learning a correction that maps the stated percentage onto the one actually observed.

It must be tested on days it was not trained on. Fitted and scored on the same days, it always looks like it helps.
Lead time

How many days ahead the forecast was made. A 3-day lead means predicted three days before the day in question.

Accuracy degrades with lead time; that degradation is usually more useful to know than any single accuracy number.
MAE / bias — Mean Absolute Error

MAE is the average size of the temperature error, ignoring direction. Bias is the average signed error.

They answer different questions. A forecast can have zero bias and still be wildly wrong daily, if errors cancel out.
Representativeness

The forecast covers a grid square of several kilometres; the rain gauge is a single point.

A summer shower can soak the gauge and miss the rest of the square, or vice versa. This looks like forecast error but is not.
ERA5 / reanalysis

A best-estimate reconstruction of past weather, blending a model with observations.

Used only as a cross-check here. Scoring a forecast against a reanalysis from the same centre flatters the forecast, so real station measurements are the primary truth.
Present weather — WMO code table 4677

A code an observer files for what the sky is doing right now: clear, mist, fog, drizzle, rain, snow, thunderstorm.

Used as the hourly truth, because Bucharest stations do not report hourly rain amounts at all. It records whether precipitation is falling, not how much - which actually matches what a probability of precipitation claims.
Weather model — also: NWP model

A computer simulation of the atmosphere. It divides the world into grid squares, applies the laws of physics step by step, and turns today's observations into tomorrow's weather.

Different weather services run different models - different grid sizes, different physics approximations, different ways of using the same starting observations. Two models can therefore give two different rain probabilities for the same city, and both can be honest.
Verification

Checking forecasts against what actually happened, measured independently - here, rain gauges and weather stations.

A forecast can be detailed, confident and confidently wrong. Verification is the only way to tell skill from confidence.
Observing practice

How often, and by what method, a station files its reports.

A station reporting three times an hour catches more brief showers than one reporting once, so it records more rain for identical weather. That is a property of the observer, not the climate, and it limits how precisely two stations can be compared.
